candidates.title: US Government Accuses Russian Spacecraft of “Threatening Behavior” and Orbital “Weapons Operations”
candidates.raw_excerpt: Last Saturday, a 17,000 mph game of cat-and-mouse appears to have played out in low Earth orbit. According to new images obtained by Axios , the Russian satellite Cosmos 2612 engaged in maneuvers that brought it within less than a mile of the Swedish-made Earth observation satellite Iceye-X36. According to the outlet’s reporting, the Russian craft burned fuel in order to adjust its altitude and speed to match that of the US-operated satellite. In a post on social media , US undersecretary of state Thomas DiNanno blasted the Russian space agency for “exhibiting threatening behavior by intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite,” which he claims are “consistent with on-orbit weapons operations.” Russian officials, meanwhile, dismissed the accusation that its satellites are armed and ready for combat as “unfounded,” instead framing the event as an operation meant to counter Western intelligence sharing with the Ukrainian military. “Western countries headed by the United States continue to use loudspeaker diplomacy repeating absurd accusations about Russia’s space activity,” deputy head of Russia’s delegation to the United Nations Konstantin Vorontsov said in a statement translated by Ars Technica . The robotic vehicle's initial drogue parachute deployed successfully, but its main parafoil detached during deployment, leaving the prototype unable to slow its descent before crashing into the ground, according to ESA officials. "An independent investigation is ongoing to determine its root cause and inform the next steps." Space Rider is being developed as Europe's first reusable orbital spacecraft — an uncrewed vehicle designed to carry scientific experiments to orbit for up to two months, then return them to Earth for analysis. Its method of return, though, differs from that of any other spacecraft in operation today. Space Rider''s wingless, lifting-body design relies on a steerable parachute, or parafoil, to maneuver toward its landing area. candidates.title: On this day in space! Oct. 22, 1992: Ashes of 'Star Trek' creator Gene Roddenberry launch into space on NASA shuttle
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Oct. 22, 1992, the space shuttle Columbia launched into space with the ashes of Gene Roddenberry, the creator of " Star Trek ," aboard. During mission STS-52, NASA astronaut and shuttle commander James Wetherbee brought a small container with a portion of Roddenberry's ashes into space as part of his personal effects at the request of Roddenberry's widow, Majel Barrett . It was Roddenberry's lifelong dream to go to space, but he never got to go while he was alive. But thanks to his wife, a little bit of Roddenberry finally made it to space almost exactly one year after his death. NASA and his family didn't tell anyone about it until almost two years later in 1994. Wetherbee said he was "honored to be asked" by Barrett to carry Roddenberry's ashses on the spaceflight. "I'm just glad I was able to bring a little happiness to the family," he said, according to Newsweek . The Space Shuttle Columbia (STS-52) launches from NASA's Kennedy Space Center on Oct. 22, 1992. (Image credit: NASA) Here's why it mattered The launch of Roddenberry's ashes into space on NASA's STS-52 mission aboard the space shuttle Columbia marked the world's first " space burial ," but it wouldn't be the last. About five years after Roddenberry's memorial flight, in 1997, the space memorial company Celestis began launching a series of "burial" flights by flying capsules with human cremains on rockets . In fact, more of Roddenberry's ashes flew on Celestis' "founders flight" in April 1997 aboard an air-launched Pegasus rocket that took off from the Canary Islands in Spain. candidates.title: Australia's bizarre 'Spider Crater' seen from orbit | Space photo of the day for Oct. 22, 2026
candidates.raw_excerpt: A satellite image of "Spider Crater" in Western Australia. (Image credit: NASA Earth Observatory image by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey ) From the dangerous Sydney funnel-web to the common huntsman, Australia is home to its fair share of spiders. It even has a crater shaped like one. What is it? One stretch of the vast Western Australia wilderness is imprinted with a curious crater, which likely formed after a meteor impact hundreds of millions of years ago. Geologists think the spider-like pattern in the crater's center was created when its floor rebounded following the initial impact, NASA has said . In the hundreds of millions of years since the initial impact, erosion has continued to carve this formation into its current, signature shape. Complete with "legs," the planetary imprint has earned its name Spider Crater. This image shows the impact structure in its entirety, which stretches 8 by 7 miles (13 by 11 kilometers) in full, with the central "spider" piece measuring 2.5 miles (4 km). Why is it incredible? In this image, we can see this "spider" from space. This snapshot shows the geologic feature as captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) aboard the Landsat 9 satellite , an Earth-observing craft that launched back in 2021. The satellite, a collaborative effort between NASA and the U.S. Geological Survey, is the ninth in the Landsat Earth-observing series, which goes all the way back to the launch of Landsat 1 in 1972. On a near-weekly basis, Landsat 9 delivers observations of everything from deforestation to water quality and crop growth. The series of Landsat satellites have been a critical piece in the modern understanding of how our planet continues to change. Whether it's the repercussions of climate change or fluctuations in agriculture, observations from orbit do more than provide interesting photos of our home world; they also capture critical data.

It arrived in lunar orbit about three weeks later and dropped off the Moon Impact Probe, which crashed into the moon on Nov. 14. The rest of the Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft stayed in orbit, where it collected and transmitted data from the moon to Earth for about a year. candidates.title: Halley’s Comet Barraging Earth With Debris
candidates.raw_excerpt: Keep your eyes peeled and your binoculars primed tonight, stargazers. The distant Halley’s Comet is reminding us of its far-off presence by pelting our planet with a barrage of meteors which will make the eastern welkin blush with a cosmic light show. The meteor shower, known as the Orionids, is characterized by its fast-moving bright streaks and fireballs that can be seen for minutes at a time, with some trails staying visible even after the meteor has blinked out. And yes, you can see them with the naked eye. Though it began at the start of October and is projected to last until November 7, the shower is expected to hit peak brightness this Wednesday night and early Thursday morning. Its resplendence, however, will be challenged by a waxing gibbous Moon, which will be around 77 percent full tonight and as such fairly shiny in its own right, but will set early in the morning.  Halley’s Comet is a long period comet that takes 76 years to orbit the Sun and only makes an appearance in our skies roughly just as often. Last time it swung by was back in 1986, and it won’t return until 2061, but the Orionids, which are essentially the debris discarded by the comet as it nears our star, can be seen at other times because they linger around long after it has departed back into the void. Our planet happens to pass through this debris field twice a year, producing a meteor shower. The Orionids falls in October, and the other meteor shower, known as the Eta Aquariid, occurs in May. The streaks of light in our sky are the comet’s ejected particles burning up as they tear through our atmosphere. To watch the Orionids, NASA recommends viewing it after moonset and before dawn because of the bright gibbous Moon. That will probably be around 3:30 AM EST. You don’t need any special equipment, but you should get outside the city and go somewhere far from any sources of light pollution. candidates.raw_excerpt: The Northern suburbs of Toledo, Ohio turned into a real life Don DeLillo novel overnight, after an explosion at a chemical facility sent plumes of industrial compounds billowing into the sky. According to the local station WTOL11 , the blast happened at a chemical distribution site in Ohio’s Lucas County on Tuesday night, prompting an immediate evacuation order for anybody living within one mile of the disaster zone. Those within three miles were given an order to shelter in place. In a press conference on Wednesday, city emergency officials explained that the leaking chemical exhaust is glycidyl methacrylate, an industrial manufacturing chemical broadly suspected to be carcinogenic to humans . Maps show numerous residential neighborhoods in the immediate vicinity, the closest being a trailer park just 0.25 miles as the crow flies from the site of the chemical explosion. The nearby Ottawa river, a tributary of Lake Erie, is situated under a half mile to the South. candidates.title: 11-Foot Chunk of Chinese Rocket Crashes Down in Minnesota Cornfield
candidates.raw_excerpt: Last week, the Sheriff’s Office in Stevens County, Minnesota made a startling Facebook post. “On October 14, 2026, at approximately 3:30pm, the Stevens County Sheriff’s Office received a phone call of foreign debris that was found in a cornfield in Scott Township,” it wrote . “Upon responding, deputies confirmed that a large, metallic object, approximately 11-feet in diameter, presumably a space object, was present in the cornfield. The Sheriff’s Office is working closely with several state and federal agencies to identify and notify the owner of the debris and to plan for removal from the field.” The post, which included a photo of a banged-up metal object surrounded by yellowed stalks of corn, quickly started picking up traction on social media due to the implication that the object had come from space. Now, Ars Technica has the receipts : the object was almost certainly chunk of a Chinese Zhuque-2E rocket that launched from the Gobi Desert, deployed 10 satellites, and then headed back Earthward, where it was spotted burning up in the skies over Kansas and Minnesota . As launches get more common and rockets get larger and sturdier — the model built by LandSpace, which deposited the debris in the cornfield, is a workhorse spacecraft meant to ferry cargo to Earth’s orbit — the chances of their detritus surviving the journey back to the ground increases. These chunks of spacefaring equipment can sometimes crash down in populated areas. In 2024, a NASA component from the International Space Station withstood reentry and crashed through a home in Florida where a family was sleeping. Space wreckage has previously been discovered previously on farms in Canada and Australia . Nobody has yet been injured by a piece of falling space debris, but as commercial ambitions for Earth’s orbit increase — the Chinese rocket had been launched to deploy satellites for a connectivity constellation meant to rival SpaceX’s Starlink — it’s probably only a matter of time. candidates.title: Startup Deploys AI-Engineered Virus on Human Patient
candidates.raw_excerpt: When it comes to putting strange substances into your body in 2026, the sky’s the limit. First there were black-market Russian peptides — and now there are AI-generated viruses, which one startup claims has been used to successfully treat a bacterial infection. On Tuesday, the company called Radical Numerics published a technical paper on its website, explaining the process by which they trialed an AI-engineered viral treatment on a human subject. Targeting bacteria with special viruses isn’t new — it’s called “phage therapy,” and it involves deploying viruses that specifically target harmful microscopic organisms. But the hunt for viruses capable of locking onto a particular infection is arduous, and Radical Numerics says it’s found a way to use AI to revolutionize the process. Yet as the New York Times notes in its reporting, Radical Numerics’ research is really more like a blog post — not only was the study self-published, rather than being vetted by a scientific journal, but it hasn’t even been peer reviewed. Making matters even murkier, the company declined to share clinical information about the patient or the doctors involved with the NYT , citing the proprietary nature of a treatment it hopes to monetize. “We take our responsibility to protect patient confidentiality and maintain the trust of our clinical partners extremely seriously,” CEO of Radical Numerics Eric Nguyen told the paper. “We intend to publish our scientific findings through peer-reviewed research, with any future disclosure of clinical details subject to appropriate consent.” As Harvard microbiologist Michael Baym told the NYT , “if it works, that’s incredible,” but his “impulse is to be skeptical.” As the saying goes, extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence — and that goes double when you’re running a venture-backed commercial lab exposing sick people to AI-generated viruses. candidates.raw_excerpt: Airbus Netherlands has shipped the first lightweight Ariane 6 Vulcain Aft Bay, one of the rocket’s final Block 2 upgrades. Airbus Netherlands has delivered the first lightweight Vulcain Aft Bay for Ariane 6 as part of the rocket’s Block 2 upgrades. The total weight reduction, however, appears to be more modest than originally anticipated. In a 21 October LinkedIn post , Airbus Netherlands President Rob Postma announced that the upgraded structure, designated Flight Model 16 (FM16), was on its way to ArianeGroup in France via Rotterdam. According to Postma, the upgrade is expected to be launched for the first time aboard an Ariane 6 mission in 2027. The Vulcain Aft Bay is a structural assembly fixed to the base of Ariane 6’s main stage. It supports the Vulcain 2.1 rocket engine and transfers the thrust generated by the engine to the rocket’s main structure. The assembly currently weighs approximately five tonnes. Postma explained that the redesigned structure is 55 millimetres shorter than its predecessor and 400 kilograms lighter. This appears to be half the weight reduction the company originally expected to achieve. In July 2024, the Netherlands Space Office reported that the upgraded aft bay would be 800 kg lighter, citing Airbus Netherlands Director of Strategy, Sales and Business Development Frank Meiboom. The agency also identified FM16 as the first flight model expected to incorporate the changes. By 2025, however, that figure appeared to have already been revised downwards. An article in Leonardo Times, an aerospace magazine published by students at Delft University of Technology, reported that engineers had achieved a weight reduction of more than 550 kg following a visit to the Airbus Netherlands production facility. Postma’s announcement did not address the discrepancy between the earlier figures and the final stated weight reduction.
